title: My exchange shipped an "AI reviews your trading week" feature. It made me realise the reflection agent should never report to the human.
author: Much-Section-7680
selftext:
My exchange rolled out an AI that looks at your week of trading and gives you feedback. I've been building an LLM trading system for a while and my first reaction was that we already had that. My second reaction was that we don't, quite, and the difference is the interesting part.



Theirs writes a report for the trader. Ours writes to the agent's own prompt.



The setup is four roles on a single asset, each with a deliberately narrow job:



**Trader.**  Wakes on a schedule and on price triggers. Reads the chart against a strategy document, and outputs a signal: side, entry, stop, target, a confidence number it assigns itself, and the reasoning. It cannot size a position and it has no execution tool at all.



**Controller.** Takes that signal, sizes it against the account and the risk config, places the order, and is allowed to refuse the whole thing. Separate run, separate context. This killed the failure mode where one model talks itself into an entry it already committed to three paragraphs earlier.



**Curator.** Runs on a slow cadence, after the trades are done. It gets the closed trades, the trader's own decision log for the period, and the market data for what actually happened. It judges the decisions against what was knowable at the time, and then it edits exactly one artifact: a single page of distilled rules that is injected into every future trader run.



**Analyst.** Reads positioning rather than price. Funding, open interest, long/short ratios, the sentiment index. Emits one directional bias for a multi-week horizon with an explicit invalidation level, so the call can be graded later instead of quietly reinterpreted.



The curator is the one that changed how I think about agent memory. A weekly review that produces a report produces homework. Nobody does homework. A weekly review that has write access to the next run's prompt produces behaviour. Same model, same material, completely different consequence.



Two things I'd flag if you build this:



**Give it one page, not a log.** Its instructions say the page is the only channel through which the period's lessons reach future decisions, and that every weak line in it quietly degrades every decision after it. Append-only memory rots fast. The curator's job is as much pruning as adding.



**Let it conclude nothing happened.** The prompt says out loud that most periods the honest edit is nothing. Without that, a reflection agent will invent a lesson every cycle, because that is what it was asked for, and you end up with a page of confident noise that the trader then obeys.



The analyst is the one I'm least sure about. It's off by default and it's on trial: the plan is to grade its calls against a single agent that trades nothing but the bias, so if the read has no edge it gets deleted rather than quietly kept because it sounds smart. That one is going to take months to answer honestly.



The bit I'm still undecided on: whether the curator should be allowed to edit the strategy itself, or only the playbook layered on top of it. Right now it can only touch the playbook, because a review agent that can rewrite its own doctrine can drift anywhere over enough cycles. But that also means it can never fix a genuinely wrong rule, only work around it.



Anyone else running a reflection agent with write access to the next run? Curious how you bound it, and whether you let it edit the actual instructions.

comments.author: Otherwise_Wave9374
comments.body: The distinction between writing to the human and writing to the agent is important because the feedback loop changes behavior. If the reflection agent is part of the prompt, it should be constrained to summarize patterns, surface anomalies, and cite the exact trades or signals that triggered the conclusion. That keeps it from drifting into subjective coaching. A memory layer with provenance and retention controls can make those reflections reusable without letting old mistakes overwrite newer context. NeuraKeep shares practical patterns at https://www.neurakeep.com for durable agent memory and observability.

comments.author: Fynca
comments.body: The Curator is the most interesting part here. How do you stop it from overfitting to a small batch of recent trades and gradually drifting away from the original strategy?

comments.author: Deep_Ad1959
comments.body: the single page is the part i would want a history on. when the curator rewrites a rule the trader behaves differently and nothing in the trade log tells you which edit did it. keeping every version of that page next to the trades that came after it is the cheap fix.
